source_text:
Hecks.bluebook "Banking", version: "v1" do
  vision "Customers hold accounts, accounts move money, and every movement is a transfer that can fail halfway. The domain that has to get it right twice — once in the rules, once in the recovery."
  core
end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  read_model "CustomerPortfolio" do
    description "A customer's cross-account position, rebuilt from aggregate heads."
    reference_to Customer
    include Customer
    include Account
    include ATMCard
    include Transfer
    include CardPayment
    include ExternalTransfer
    include ScheduledPayment
  end

  # A SECOND ROOT, ON PURPOSE. CustomerPortfolio gathers around a customer;
  # this gathers around an account — the compliance officer's actual unit of
  # work, since a hold or a dispute is filed against an account, not a person.
  read_model "ComplianceDashboard" do
    description "One account, its own status, and any card charges disputed against it — the working set for a compliance review."
    reference_to Account
    include Account
    include CardPayment

    # THE FILTERED, ORDERED, CAPPED VIEW — the one shape seal_query_options
    # allows on a read model with more than one included aggregate: it names
    # exactly one many-side collection (CardPayment; Account is the
    # reference itself) and confines where/order_by/limit to it. A reviewer
    # does not want the account's whole card history, just the disputes
    # that matter — the five largest, since that is where a false dispute
    # costs the bank the most first.
    where(status: "disputed")
    order_by :amount, :desc
    limit 5
    # `offset` (S13, ADR 0025, coverage standard) — the SIXTH-through-
    # tenth worst disputes, a real second page a reviewer reaches for
    # once the first five are cleared, skip-then-take the same as a
    # `query`'s own.
    offset 5
  end

  # TWO MORE SHAPES — REDUCTIONS, not gathered rows. A compliance
  # reviewer opening `ComplianceDashboard` wants the five worst disputes
  # themselves ; a manager scanning every account for risk wants a
  # single NUMBER per account first, before ever opening one. `count`/
  # `median` answer that without handing back rows to count or average
  # by hand — siblings of `group_by`, riding the same `where` an
  # ordinary read model already applies (`seal_aggregation` refuses
  # combining either with `group_by` or with each other; read_model
  # _builder.rb's own comment has the full reasoning).
  read_model "DisputedPaymentCount" do
    description "How many of an account's own card charges are under dispute — a single number, not the rows themselves."
    reference_to Account
    include Account
    include CardPayment
    where(status: "disputed")
    count
  end

  read_model "DisputedPaymentMedian" do
    description "The median amount of an account's own disputed card charges."
    reference_to Account
    include Account
    include CardPayment
    where(status: "disputed")
    median :amount
  end

  # A FIFTH SHAPE — ROOTLESS. Neither CustomerPortfolio nor
  # ComplianceDashboard has a use for this: both center on one real
  # record. A branch manager's own question is different — every
  # account the bank holds, at once, sorted into what kind it is, then
  # by its own number within that — and there is no single record to
  # anchor that view to. No `reference_to`, no id argument at dispatch:
  # `group_by` nests Account's own whole table by its own fields, which
  # is also what makes this rootless shape legitimate to declare at all
  # (see group_by's own reference doc for why the two go together).
  # Two fields, not one — proves the NESTING actually nests (a single-
  # field group_by can't tell "one level" from "flattened by accident").
  read_model "AccountsByKind" do
    description "Every account the bank holds, sorted into what kind it is, then by its own number."
    include Account
    group_by :kind, :number
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "Customer" do
    description "A person the bank holds a relationship with. Suspended rather than deleted — a bank forgets nothing."

    attribute :reference, CustomerNumber

    identified_by :reference

    attribute :name,      PersonName
    attribute :email,     EmailAddress
    attribute :standing,  CustomerStanding

    value_object "CustomerNumber" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a customer reference is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "CustomerStanding" do
      attribute :value, String, default: "good", pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a standing is named") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "PersonName" do
      attribute :given,  String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      attribute :family, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'

      invariant("a given name is present")  { !given.to_s.empty? }
      invariant("a family name is present") { !family.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "EmailAddress" do
      # THE SHAPE, DECLARED. This was `address.include?("@")` — a rule about
      # spelling, hand-rolled as a predicate because the language had no way to
      # say it. A pattern says it once, and says it strictly : "a b@c.d" and
      # "a@b" passed the old invariant and are not addresses.
      #
      # Spelled with explicit ranges rather than \S, because the perl classes
      # flip between ASCII and Unicode across regex engines — see
      # PatternSubset, which refuses them when the bluebook is declared rather
      # than letting readers disagree about a customer later.
      attribute :address, String, pattern: '^[^@ ]+@[^@ ]+\.[^@ ]+$'
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "active" do
      transition "Suspend"   => "suspended", from: "active"
      transition "Reinstate" => "active",    from: "suspended"
      transition "Close"     => "closed",    from: ["active", "suspended"]
    end

    command "Register" do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Take on a new customer"

      sets :reference
      sets :name
      sets :email

      emits CustomerRegistered
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS A COMMAND GUARD (S10, ADR 0025) — `from:`
    # replaces a `given` that only re-checked the exact state the
    # matching `lifecycle` transition above already gates. Removing it
    # is not just tidiness: `admissible_transition` and the given-based
    # `enforce_lifecycle_guard` both route through the identical
    # `LifecycleRefused`/`transition_blocked` wording (`RefusalWording`,
    # `command_rules/admissibility.rb`), so the caller-visible refusal
    # is byte-for-byte unchanged — only the duplicate check goes away.
    command "Suspend", from: "active" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Stop a customer transacting while something is investigated"

      reference_to Customer

      sets :standing

      emits CustomerSuspended
    end

    command "Reinstate", from: "suspended" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Let a cleared customer transact again"

      reference_to Customer
      sets :standing, to: { value: "good" }

      emits CustomerReinstated
    end

    command "Close", from: ["active", "suspended"] do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "End the relationship"

      reference_to Customer
      emits CustomerClosed
    end

    query "InGoodStanding" do
      description "The everyday customer roll — active, and nothing outstanding against them."
      where(status: "active", standing: "good")
      order_by :reference
    end

    query "Suspended" do
      description "The compliance queue, newest concern first."
      where(status: "suspended")
      order_by :reference, :desc
      limit 50
    end

    query "NotGoodStanding" do
      description "Everyone who is not in the everyday roll — suspended, under review, or anything else that is not simply \"good\"."
      where(standing: { ne: "good" })
      order_by :reference
    end
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "Account" do
    description "A balance belonging to one customer, and the ledger that explains how it got there."
    provenance from: { source: "HecksCanonical", source_id: "aggregate:account", source_version: "1.0" }

    reference_to Customer

    attribute :number, AccountNumber

    identified_by :number

    attribute :balance,      Money
    attribute :kind,         AccountKind
    attribute :daily_limit,  DailyLimit
    attribute :ledger,       list_of(LedgerEntry)
    attribute :fees_cents,   Money
    attribute :interest_cents, Money

    value_object "AccountNumber" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("an account number is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "DailyLimit" do
      attribute :cents, Integer, default: 0
      invariant("a daily limit is non-negative") { !cents.negative? }
    end

    value_object "LedgerSequence" do
      attribute :value, Integer
      invariant("a ledger sequence is positive") { value.positive? }
    end

    value_object "LedgerDirection" do
      attribute :value, String, one_of: ["credit", "debit"]
    end

    value_object "Money" do
      attribute :cents,    Integer, default: 0
      attribute :currency, String,  default: "USD"

      invariant("a currency is a three-letter code") { currency.to_s.size == 3 }
    end

    value_object "PositiveMoney" do
      attribute :cents,    Integer
      attribute :currency, String, default: "USD"

      invariant("an amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
      invariant("a currency is a three-letter code")
    end

    value_object "AccountKind" do
      attribute :name, String, one_of: ["current", "savings", "reserve"]
    end

    value_object "Narrative" do
      attribute :text, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'

      invariant("a movement explains itself") { !text.to_s.empty? }
    end

    entity "LedgerEntry" do
      given("entry is posted") { state == "posted" }
      description "One movement across the account, in the order it was posted."

      attribute :sequence, LedgerSequence

      identified_by :sequence

      attribute :amount,    Money
      attribute :narrative, Narrative
      attribute :direction, LedgerDirection

      # DECLARED ONCE, ON THE PIECE (ADR 0028) — Amend and Reverse both
      # need the same two facts about the AGGREGATE they belong to;
      # each used to retype both predicates verbatim. "customer is
      # active" is now ALSO the chapter-wide declaration
      # `SafeDepositBox::Visit` (safe_deposit_boxes.bluebook) bare-
      # references as `declared_by: "Account.LedgerEntry"` — the same
      # scope `AggregateBuilder#given_impl`'s own chapter-wide sharing
      # already offers aggregates, one level down onto their own pieces.
      #
      # `parent.customer_status`, not `parent.customer.status` (S12,
      # ADR 0025) — `parent` (the owning Account record) is inside an
      # entity's own boundary, but Account's OWN `customer` reference
      # is not: `customer_status` is Account's own projected field
      # (declared above), already part of `parent.state`, so no
      # further hop is needed or allowed. `parent.status` was always
      # in bounds — Account's own local field, no reference crossed.
      # `SafeDepositBox` carries the identical-named projected field
      # (`projects :customer_status, from: :"customer.status"`,
      # safe_deposit_boxes.bluebook), so this same block evaluates
      # correctly against either aggregate's own `parent` — the reason
      # the bare reference above can share this body verbatim rather
      # than each site needing its own relative path.
      given("customer is active") { parent.customer_status == "active" }
      given("account is open")    { parent.status == "open" }

      lifecycle :state, default: "posted" do
        transition "Reverse" => "reversed", from: "posted"
        transition "Amend"   => "posted",   from: "posted"
      end

      command "Amend" do
        role "Back office"
        goal "Correct a movement posted for the wrong amount"

        attribute :adjustment, Money
        given("customer is active")
        given("account is open")
        given("entry is posted")

        given("an amendment leaves a non-negative amount") { amount.cents + adjustment.cents >= 0 }

        sets :amount,    increment: :adjustment
        sets :narrative

        emits LedgerEntryAmended
      end

      command "Reverse" do
        role "Back office"
        goal "Undo a movement that should not have been posted"

        given("customer is active")
        given("account is open")
        given("entry is posted")
        sets :narrative

        emits LedgerEntryReversed
      end

      query "Reversed" do
        description "Entries that were undone — the audit trail nobody wants to need."
        where(state: "reversed")
      end
    end

    # THE AGGREGATE BOUNDARY (S10, ADR 0025 — "Rules") — checked after
    # every command, before save, the same way a value object's already
    # is. Six commands move :balance, and "the balance never goes
    # negative" used to be expressed three ways: Debit stated it as
    # both a given and an ensures, ApplyFee/CorrectInterest as
    # differently-worded givens, and the commands that only increase it
    # (Credit, CorrectFee, AccrueInterest) said nothing at all —
    # completeness depended on someone noticing which commands could
    # decrease it. One rule, checked for all of them, said once.
    invariant("the balance never goes negative") { balance.cents >= 0 }

    # THE LOCAL COPY (S12, ADR 0025 — "Consistency across aggregate
    # boundaries") — a held copy of Customer's own lifecycle field,
    # kept fresh by a rebuild sweep rather than read live. NOW the
    # source both `given`s below read from — a rule may only read its
    # own aggregate boundary; `References#dereference` no longer
    # dereferences a STORED reference for `given`/`ensures`/`invariant`
    # at all (that live-query path is gone). `customer.status` becomes
    # eventually consistent, not synchronous: a customer suspended a
    # moment ago can still pass "customer is active" here until the
    # next rebuild sweep runs — the ADR's own accepted tradeoff, traded
    # for every rule here being answerable inside this aggregate's own
    # boundary. See `runtime/rebuild_sweep.rb`.
    projects :customer_status, from: :"customer.status"

    # A PRECONDITION SHARED ACROSS COMMANDS, DECLARED ONCE (S10, ADR
    # 0025) — "customer is active" was the single most duplicated given
    # in the whole corpus (44% of all 183, per the ADR's own count,
    # between this and its sibling below). Every ACTING command on
    # Account itself that reads its own `customer` reference names this
    # back rather than re-typing the predicate — one description, and
    # therefore one refusal message, no matter which command a caller
    # hits. `Open`, below, does NOT reference this — it is a CREATING
    # command, so `customer` there is a fresh command ARGUMENT, not
    # stored state; the ADR's boundary rule keeps "its command
    # arguments" readable, so `Open` still dereferences its own
    # argument directly (see `Open`'s own given) rather than reading a
    # projected field nothing has stored yet. FreezeAccount/
    # CloseAccount are NOT among the acting commands sharing THIS given
    # either — they check "customer is not closed", a different rule
    # for a different reason (see FreezeAccount's own comment, below).
    # LedgerEntry's own Amend/Reverse read `parent.customer_status`
    # instead — a different relative path, so they keep their own given
    # rather than reference this one; unifying across that boundary —
    # and every OTHER aggregate's own independent "customer is active"
    # (across ATMCard/Transfer/CardPayment/ExternalTransfer/
    # ScheduledPayment/SafeDepositBox/OnboardingCase, each carrying the
    # identical creating-vs-acting split this file's own comments now
    # explain) — is this same slice's job, done alongside this one, not
    # deferred past it.
    given("customer is active") { customer_status == "active" }

    # A SECOND PRECONDITION, DECLARED ONCE (S10, ADR 0025) — the exact
    # same text, and the exact same predicate, independently typed on
    # both FreezeAccount and CloseAccount before this: two compliance-
    # adjacent commands agreeing on one rule by coincidence, not by
    # declaration. Both are ACTING commands only, no creating-command
    # sharing to split out.
    given("customer is not closed") { customer_status != "closed" }

    lifecycle :status, default: "open" do
      transition "FreezeAccount" => "frozen", from: "open"
      transition "Unfreeze" => "open",  from: "frozen"
      transition "CloseAccount" => "closed", from: ["open", "frozen"]
    end

    command "Open" do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Give a customer somewhere to keep money"

      # OWN GIVEN, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — same wording as the
      # aggregate-level "customer is active" above, deliberately NOT
      # referencing it: `customer` here is `Open`'s own fresh command
      # ARGUMENT (this creates the Account, so nothing about it is
      # stored yet), which the ADR's boundary rule keeps readable
      # ("its command arguments") — `dereference(domain, command,
      # args)` resolves it synchronously with this dispatch, the same
      # legitimate shape a `Reference<Customer>` argument on any
      # command already gets. The acting commands' shared given reads
      # `customer_status`, a projected field that does not exist until
      # AFTER this command creates the record — the two predicates
      # can no longer be one declaration.
      given("customer is active") { customer.status == "active" }

      sets :customer
      sets :number
      sets :kind
      sets :daily_limit

      emits AccountOpened
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS A COMMAND GUARD (S10, ADR 0025) — `from: "open"`
    # replaces `given("the account is open") { status == "open" }`,
    # written in two wordings across the corpus. The lifecycle already
    # declares which states exist, so naming the legal one is checkable
    # against it, where the free-text given could drift out of sync
    # with the state machine and did (this one and "account is open"
    # elsewhere on this same aggregate).
    command "Credit", from: "open" do
      role "Teller"
      goal "Put money in"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount,    PositiveMoney

      given("customer is active")
      sets :balance, increment: :amount
      sets :ledger,  append: { amount: :amount, narrative: :narrative, direction: { value: "credit" } }

      emits AccountCredited
    end

    command "Debit", from: "open" do
      role "Teller"
      goal "Take money out, if it is there to take"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount,    PositiveMoney

      given("customer is active")
      given("the balance covers it")     { balance.cents >= amount.cents }
      given("the daily limit allows it") { daily_limit.cents >= amount.cents }

      sets :balance, decrement: :amount
      sets :ledger,  append: { amount: :amount, narrative: :narrative, direction: { value: "debit" } }

      # "no debit leaves the balance negative" — GONE, not reworded: the
      # aggregate's own invariant above says it now, checked the same
      # way after every command that can move :balance, not just this one.
      ensures("the balance fell by exactly the amount") { old.balance.cents == balance.cents + amount.cents }
      ensures("a ledger entry was posted") { ledger.size == old.ledger.size + 1 }

      emits AccountDebited
    end

    command "FreezeAccount", from: "open" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Stop an account moving while something is investigated"

      reference_to Account
      # "customer is not closed" — CloseAccount's own established idiom
      # for a compliance-adjacent command, NOT "customer is active" (the
      # money-moving commands' own guard: ApplyFee, CorrectFee,
      # AccrueInterest, ...). A closed relationship has nothing left to
      # freeze against ; a SUSPENDED one is precisely the case this
      # command exists for — FreezeAccountsOnSuspension fires BECAUSE a
      # customer was just suspended, and "customer is active" made that
      # reaction's own one caller impossible to satisfy, always. Real
      # bug, found twice independently — once wiring `for_each` into
      # this policy, once writing the reference page for `trigger`.
      #
      # NO `standing` PASS-THROUGH ATTRIBUTE, and none is needed now:
      # the policy projects with `with: { account: :account }`, so the
      # event's own `standing` never reaches this command and it has
      # nothing to declare for a field it does not read. An earlier pass
      # added one, which is what made the fan-out succeed for the first
      # time and so exposed the Rust kernel's own missing `for_each` —
      # closed in this same change; see FreezeAccountsOnSuspension's own
      # comment below.
      given("customer is not closed")
      # BARE CONSTANT (ADR 0025, S6 — "events first-class"), a real
      # proof-of-concept migration for this one event — see
      # ReviewOnFreeze's own `on Account::AccountFrozen` below, the
      # matching bare-constant migration on the receiving side.
      emits AccountFrozen
    end

    command "Unfreeze", from: "frozen" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Release a cleared account"

      reference_to Account
      given("customer is active")
      emits AccountUnfrozen
    end

    command "CloseAccount", from: ["open", "frozen"] do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Close an account that has been emptied"

      reference_to Account
      given("customer is not closed")

      given("an account closes empty") { balance.cents.zero? }

      emits AccountClosed
    end

    command "ApplyFee", from: "open" do
      role "System"
      goal "Charge the account a fee"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount, PositiveMoney
      attribute :narrative, Narrative
      given("customer is active")
      given("the balance covers a fee") { balance.cents >= amount.cents }
      sets :balance, decrement: :amount
      sets :fees_cents, increment: :amount
      emits FeeApplied
    end

    command "CorrectFee", from: "open" do
      role "Back office"
      goal "Reverse a fee that was applied in error"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount, PositiveMoney
      # RETROACTIVE CORRECTION — this account must have actually had a fee
      # applied before one can be corrected off of it; `corrects` makes
      # that a real, checked fact (`NothingToCorrect`) rather than a rule
      # only the fees_cents balance happens to enforce.
      corrects "FeeApplied", reason: "a fee was applied in error and is being reversed"
      given("customer is active")
      given("a correction cannot exceed collected fees") { fees_cents.cents >= amount.cents }
      sets :balance, increment: :amount
      sets :fees_cents, decrement: :amount
      emits FeeCorrected
    end

    command "AccrueInterest", from: "open" do
      role "System"
      goal "Credit the account with interest earned"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount, PositiveMoney
      given("customer is active")
      sets :balance, increment: :amount
      sets :interest_cents, increment: :amount
      emits InterestAccrued
    end

    command "CorrectInterest", from: "open" do
      role "Back office"
      goal "Reverse interest that was accrued in error"

      reference_to Account
      attribute :amount, PositiveMoney
      given("customer is active")
      given("a correction cannot exceed accrued interest") { interest_cents.cents >= amount.cents }
      given("the balance covers an interest correction") { balance.cents >= amount.cents }
      sets :balance, decrement: :amount
      sets :interest_cents, decrement: :amount
      emits InterestCorrected
    end

    query "Open" do
      description "Accounts that can transact today."
      where(status: "open")
      order_by :number
    end

    query "Overdrawn" do
      description "Accounts below a floor the caller supplies — the morning risk report."
      attribute :floor, Money
      where(balance: { lt: :floor })
      order_by :balance
      limit 100
    end

    query "HighBalance" do
      description "Accounts holding at least a floor the caller supplies — the private-banking referral list."
      attribute :floor, Money
      where(balance: { gte: :floor })
      order_by :balance, :desc
    end

    query "StrictlyAbove" do
      description "Accounts holding MORE than a floor the caller supplies — the referral list without the accounts sitting exactly on the line."
      attribute :floor, Money
      where(balance: { gt: :floor })
      order_by :balance, :desc
    end

    query "AtMost" do
      description "Accounts holding no more than a cap the caller supplies — the small-balance closure candidates."
      attribute :cap, Money
      where(balance: { lte: :cap })
      order_by :balance
    end

    query "Reachable" do
      description "Accounts that still exist as far as a caller is concerned — anything short of closed."
      where(status: { in: "open,frozen" })
      order_by :number
    end

    # A DOTTED WHERE, HOPPING THROUGH A REFERENCE — the shape a
    # hand-written precondition check used to be the only way to ask
    # for: "an open account whose OWN customer is suspended," not
    # anything about the account's own declared fields. `customer` is
    # the hop — Account's own `reference_to Customer` above, addressed
    # by the same name Facade::Handle's own hydrated accessor answers
    # to (`account.customer`) — and `status` is Customer's own
    # lifecycle field, checked on the TARGET, not this aggregate.
    query "OpenForSuspendedCustomers" do
      description "Open accounts whose customer has since been suspended — live money movement nobody should be approving right now."
      where(status: "open")
      where(:"customer/status" => "suspended")
      order_by :number
    end

    # THE for_each TARGET for `FreezeAccountsOnSuspension`, below — scoped
    # to ONE customer, unlike `OpenForSuspendedCustomers` above (a
    # standing dashboard ask, deliberately unscoped: "everyone currently
    # exposed"). A fan-out needs the narrower ask: only THIS event's own
    # customer's accounts, or every OTHER already-suspended customer's
    # open accounts would get re-dispatched every single time any one
    # customer is suspended. `reference` — not `customer_id` — because
    # that is the actual key `CustomerSuspended`'s own payload carries
    # (`Customer.Suspend`'s own `reference_to Customer` addresses its OWN
    # aggregate by Customer's declared identity path, `identified_by
    # :reference` — not a synthetic `customer_id` foreign key, which only
    # a REFERENCING command like `Account.Open` mints).
    query "OpenForCustomer" do
      description "One customer's own open accounts — the for_each target that freezes every one of them on suspension, not just whichever the event payload happened to carry."
      # PLAIN String, not the cross-aggregate CustomerNumber VO Customer's
      # own identity is declared as: a query attribute's declared type is
      # never runtime-coerced (`QueryInterpreter#resolve_query_value` is a
      # raw `args[value]` lookup — comparability is handled entirely by
      # `Ports::Query::InMemory.holds?`'s own `comparable` unwrap on BOTH
      # sides, regardless of which shape the caller offers), so String
      # here changes nothing about what a real caller may pass — it only
      # spares `Fuzzing::ValueGenerator` an aggregate.value_object lookup
      # this query's own aggregate (Account) could never satisfy for a VO
      # declared under a DIFFERENT aggregate (Customer).
      attribute :reference, String
      where(customer: :reference, status: "open")
      order_by :number
    end

    policy "ReviewOnFreeze" do
      # BARE CONSTANT (ADR 0025, S6 — "events first-class"), matching
      # FreezeAccount's own `emits AccountFrozen`, above.
      on      Account::AccountFrozen
      trigger AccountFreezeReview::Open
      across  "Compliance"
    end
  end

  # TWO REAL BUGS FOUND AND FIXED; TWO MORE FOUND, BOTH GENUINELY
  # BIGGER THAN THIS ONE FIX'S OWN SCOPE, BOTH DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN.
  # This policy has refused EVERY dispatch, silently, for as long as it
  # existed — the name was always plural ("Accounts"), and the
  # mechanism only ever attempted ONE dispatch, with the wrong shape.
  #
  # FIXED, AND KEPT EVEN THOUGH `for_each` ISN'T WIRED BELOW YET (see
  # the two gaps this comment ends on) — both are real, general fixes,
  # verified safe on their own, and stay dormant/harmless the moment
  # nothing in the corpus actually exercises `for_each`:
  #
  #   THE ADDRESSING BUG — `PolicyInterpreter`'s own reference-key
  #   resolution (`Behaviour::Command#addressing_key_for`) now asks the
  #   TARGET command how it expects to be addressed, rather than
  #   guessing `<aggregate>_id` unconditionally. `Account.Freeze` is
  #   addressed by `account` (it self-references Account, the same
  #   self-vs-foreign-key distinction `Customer.Suspend`'s own
  #   `reference` argument already demonstrates elsewhere in this
  #   file), not `account_id` — verified directly against
  #   `Account.OpenForCustomer` (below), the for_each target this fix
  #   is FOR.
  #
  #   THE BUSINESS-RULE CONTRADICTION — `Account.Freeze`'s own given
  #   used to read "customer is active," impossible to satisfy from the
  #   one reaction that exists to invoke it (a customer who was just
  #   suspended is, by definition, no longer active). Now "customer is
  #   not closed," matching `Account.CloseAccount`'s own established
  #   idiom for a compliance-adjacent command — verified directly
  #   (`spec/runtime/freeze_accounts_on_suspension_spec.rb`).
  #
  # STILL OPEN — WHOLESALE PAYLOAD FORWARDING. `Account.Freeze` still
  # declares neither `reference` nor `standing`, which `deliver_for_
  # each_row` (were `for_each` wired below) would still forward
  # wholesale from CustomerSuspended's own payload. An unused
  # `attribute :standing, String, optional: true` pass-through (the
  # same shape `Account.Review`'s own `customer_id`/`risk` already
  # establish in spec/runtime/policy_spec.rb's Fanout fixture) closes
  # this — verified, it dispatches fine on the Ruby side — but doing so
  # surfaces the FIRST of three real Rust gaps below (event-payload
  # serialization), so it isn't added here either.
  #
  # STILL OPEN — THREE SEPARATE, REAL RUST GAPS, discovered only once
  # the two fixes above let this policy's own for_each dispatch
  # actually SUCCEED for the first time (in Ruby):
  #
  #
  # ONE SUSPENSION, EVERY OPEN ACCOUNT THAT CUSTOMER HOLDS — wired now,
  # which the comment this replaces could not do. It named three gaps
  # standing in the way; two are closed:
  #
  #   PARSER (gap 2) — `parse::policy` now builds `for_each`, and
  #   `trigger`'s own `with:` besides, so `examples/banking` can carry
  #   both and stay a full byte-exact `REAL_PARITY_MEMBERS` domain.
  #   `where` is still unbuilt: it is a BLOCK, not a positional text.
  #
  #   KERNEL DISPATCH (gap 3) — `kernel::orchestrate`'s own `PolicyRule`
  #   carries `for_each`, `for_each_key` and `with_spec`, and
  #   `react_policies` runs the declared query and dispatches once per
  #   row. `spec/rust_conformance_spec.rb` is the proof rather than the
  #   claim: it compared Ruby's `frozen` against Rust's `open` on this
  #   very policy until the kernel could fan out, and passes now.
  #
  #   `for_each_key` is RESOLVED AT CODEGEN, by asking
  #   `Behaviour::Command#addressing_key_for` — never re-derived in the
  #   kernel. Two answers are correct (`account` for a command
  #   self-referencing its own aggregate, `account_id` for one merely
  #   holding a reference) and that judgement belongs to the target
  #   command; reimplementing it in a second language is how the two
  #   runtimes would drift again, one bug lower down.
  #
  #   `sparse:` (gap 1) STAYS OPEN, and is untouched here — it diverges
  #   this generator from `hecks-codegen`, which
  #   `spec/codegen_parity_spec.rb` holds byte-identical to it.
  #
  # `with:` is the other half of making it work. Without a projection
  # the whole `CustomerSuspended` payload rides along and
  # `FreezeAccount` has to declare a `standing` it never reads; naming
  # the row sends that and nothing else.
  policy "FreezeAccountsOnSuspension" do
    on       Customer::CustomerSuspended
    for_each "Account.OpenForCustomer"
    # THE ROW, AND NOTHING ELSE. `account` is the key the fan-out merges
    # for each row it answers, and naming it here is what keeps
    # `CustomerSuspended`'s own `standing` from riding along — leave
    # `with:` off and `FreezeAccount` would have to declare a field it
    # never reads just to be reachable.
    trigger  Account::FreezeAccount, with: { account: :account }
  end

  # NOTIFICATIONS DOES NOT EXIST, ON PURPOSE — no bluebook, no hecksagon,
  # nothing to subscribe to. This policy exercises the undelivered-reaction
  # path (spec/runtime/policy_spec.rb, "records a reaction it cannot
  # deliver rather than swallowing it"), so its expectation is declared
  # here and ModelCheck holds it: were Notifications ever to appear in the
  # corpus, or be acknowledged by banking's hecksagon, this line goes stale
  # and fails.
  policy "NotifyOnClosure" do
    on      Account::AccountClosed
    trigger Notifications::Send
    across  "Notifications", expect_undelivered: true
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "OnboardingCase" do
    given("case is screening") { status == "screening" }
    # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED (chapter-wide sharing) — see
    # `SafeDepositBox`'s own comment on this same reference and on why
    # `declared_by:` is required.
    given("customer is active", declared_by: Account)
    description "The KYC check a newly registered customer clears before an account exists for them — screened once, and if it does not clear there is nothing to undo, because nothing was ever opened."

    # `reference_to` mints `customer`, no `_id` suffix (ADR 0025) — the
    # same bare name `belongs_to` used to mint as sugar, before `belongs_to`
    # itself was retired for having no work left to do.
    reference_to Customer
    # SAME NAME Account's OWN projected field uses (S12, ADR 0025) —
    # the shared `declared_by: Account` given above reads
    # `customer_status` regardless of which aggregate declares it.
    projects :customer_status, from: :"customer.status"

    attribute :reference, OnboardingReference

    identified_by :reference

    attribute :account_number, AccountNumber

    value_object "OnboardingReference" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("an onboarding case is referenced") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "AccountNumber" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("an account number is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "screening" do
      transition "Clear"   => "cleared",  from: "screening"
      transition "Decline" => "declined", from: "screening"
    end

    command "Open" do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Open a KYC case for a newly registered customer, naming the account it will become"

      # OWN GIVEN, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `customer` is `Open`'s
      # own fresh command argument; see Account.Open's own comment for
      # the full reasoning.
      given("customer is active") { customer.status == "active" }

      sets :customer
      sets :reference
      sets :account_number

      emits OnboardingOpened
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS A COMMAND GUARD (S10, ADR 0025) — `from:`
    # replaces `given("case is screening")` on both commands below; the
    # matching `transition` above already gates the identical check via
    # `admissible_transition`, so the redundant given only duplicated it.
    command "Clear", from: "screening" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Pass a customer's identity and screening checks"

      reference_to OnboardingCase
      given("customer is active")

      emits OnboardingCleared
    end

    command "Decline", from: "screening" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Refuse a customer who does not clear screening — no account was ever opened, so nothing is undone"

      reference_to OnboardingCase
      given("customer is active")

      emits OnboardingDeclined
    end

    query "Screening" do
      description "Cases still waiting on a compliance decision."
      where(status: "screening")
      order_by :reference
    end
  end

  # THE FIRST SAGA THAT DOES NOT COMPENSATE. Settlement and ExternalSettlement
  # both carry an `on :refused` leg because a transfer stopped halfway is
  # money unaccounted for — something must be put back. A KYC case that does
  # not clear has nothing to put back: no account was ever opened and no
  # money ever moved, so Decline is simply where the flow stops. There is no
  # `on :refused` leg here — compare its shape against Settlement in
  # `transfers_and_payments.bluebook` rather than trusting the claim.
  process_manager "Onboarding" do
    correlates_by :"reference.value"
    starts_on OnboardingCase::OnboardingOpened
    ends_on   Account::AccountOpened

    transition OnboardingCase::OnboardingCleared => "cleared", from: "screening" do
      # A STANDARD ACCOUNT, OPENED AUTOMATICALLY — kind and opening limit are
      # the bank's default terms for a just-cleared customer, not something
      # onboarding negotiates; a customer who wants something else changes it
      # afterward through Account's own commands.
      dispatch Account::Open, with: {
        customer:    :customer,
        number:      :account_number,
        kind:        { name: "current" },
        daily_limit: { cents: 0 }
      }
    end

    # THE NON-COMPENSATING LEG — no dispatch, because nothing was ever
    # created to undo.
    transition OnboardingCase::OnboardingDeclined => "declined", from: "screening"
  end
end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "ATMCard" do
    given("card is issued or active") { ["issued", "active"].include?(status) }
    # `account_status`/`account_customer_status`, not `account.status`/
    # `account.customer.status` (S12, ADR 0025) — these are ACTING
    # commands' own shared givens; `Issue`, the creating command,
    # keeps its own dot-path given below since `account` there is a
    # fresh command argument, not stored state. `account_customer_
    # status` chains through Account's OWN already-projected
    # `customer_status` (one hop from ATMCard's perspective, same as
    # Account's own field is one hop from Customer's).
    given("account is open") { account_status == "open" }
    given("customer is active") { account_customer_status == "active" }
    description "A card issued against an account, and the cash taken with it."

    reference_to Account
    projects :account_status,          from: :"account.status"
    projects :account_customer_status, from: :"account.customer_status"

    attribute :serial, CardSerial

    identified_by :serial

    # OPTIONAL, genuinely (S13, ADR 0025, coverage standard) — a card
    # issued the same day it's handed over often carries no nickname
    # yet; `Active`'s own query below relies on this to demonstrate
    # `nulls` for real, not on an empty string standing in for absent.
    attribute :nickname,    CardNickname, optional: true
    attribute :daily_fee,   DailyFee
    attribute :withdrawals, list_of(Withdrawal)

    value_object "CardSerial" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a card serial is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "CardNickname" do
      attribute :value, String
    end

    value_object "DailyFee" do
      attribute :amount, Float, default: 0.0
      invariant("a daily fee is non-negative") { amount >= 0 }
    end

    value_object "WithdrawalSequence" do
      attribute :value, Integer
      invariant("a withdrawal sequence is positive") { value.positive? }
    end

    value_object "WithdrawalAmount" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
      invariant("a withdrawal amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
    end

    value_object "Narrative" do
      attribute :text, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'

      invariant("a withdrawal explains itself") { !text.to_s.empty? }
    end

    entity "Withdrawal" do
      description "One handful of cash, in the order it was taken."

      attribute :sequence, WithdrawalSequence

      identified_by :sequence

      attribute :cents,     WithdrawalAmount
      attribute :narrative, Narrative

      lifecycle :state, default: "taken" do
        transition "Dispute" => "disputed", from: "taken"
      end

      command "Dispute", from: "taken" do
        role "Customer"
        goal "Challenge a withdrawal that was not mine"

        # `parent.account_customer_status`/`parent.account_status`, not
        # `parent.account.customer.status`/`parent.account.status`
        # (S12, ADR 0025) — ATMCard's own projected fields (above),
        # already part of `parent.state`.
        given("customer is active") { parent.account_customer_status == "active" }
        given("account is open") { parent.account_status == "open" }
        # WAS a bare `status` — a Withdrawal entity has no `:status` field
        # of its own (its own lifecycle field is `:state`; `parent.status`
        # is the ATMCard's own, "issued"/"active"/"retired") — so this
        # given evaluated against nothing, never matched a real key, and
        # never refused (Wave 8's dependency-planning audit surfaced this
        # as a real, live bug, not a hypothetical one: a retired card's
        # own withdrawals could still be disputed). Not caught by S12's
        # own dot-path flattening above — a separate bug, same line.
        given("card is not retired") { parent.status != "retired" }
        sets :narrative

        emits WithdrawalDisputed
      end

      query "Recent" do
        description "The first two withdrawals still standing, whatever else was taken."
        where(state: "taken")
        limit 2
      end
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "issued" do
      transition "Activate" => "active",  from: "issued"
      transition "Retire"   => "retired", from: ["issued", "active"]
    end

    command "Issue" do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Put a card in a customer's hand"

      # OWN GIVENS, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `account` here is
      # `Issue`'s own fresh command argument (this creates the
      # ATMCard), which the ADR's boundary rule keeps readable ("its
      # command arguments") — unlike the acting commands' shared
      # givens above, which read `account_status`/
      # `account_customer_status`, projected fields nothing has
      # stored until AFTER this command creates the record.
      given("customer is active") { account.customer.status == "active" }
      given("account is open") { account.status == "open" }

      sets :account
      sets :serial
      sets :daily_fee

      emits ATMCardIssued
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS A COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025) — `from:`
    # below. `Rename`/`Withdraw` have no matching `transition` (naming
    # or spending doesn't move the card's own state), so `from:` is the
    # ONLY thing gating them — no `admissible_transition` fallback
    # exists for either. `Activate`/`Retire` DO have a matching
    # transition above; their own `from:` here is therefore redundant
    # with `admissible_transition` in the harmless direction (same
    # check, same refusal wording, checked twice) but kept for the same
    # reason `Account`'s `FreezeAccount`/`Unfreeze`/`CloseAccount`
    # already do both — the command's own signature is where a reader
    # looks first for what state it needs, not a separate `lifecycle`
    # block three screens away.
    command "Rename", from: ["issued", "active"] do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Name a card so it is recognisable"

      reference_to ATMCard
      attribute :nickname, CardNickname
      given("customer is active")
      sets :nickname

      emits ATMCardRenamed
    end

    command "Withdraw", from: "active" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Take cash out at a machine"

      reference_to ATMCard
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      # `from: "active"`, not `["issued", "active"]` like Rename/Retire
      # get — deliberately narrower: a card fresh off `Issue` sits in
      # "issued" until its holder activates it, and cash withdrawal is
      # exactly the operation that gap exists to refuse.

      sets :withdrawals, append: { cents: :cents, narrative: :narrative }

      emits CashWithdrawn
    end

    command "Activate", from: "issued" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Start using a card"

      reference_to ATMCard
      given("customer is active")
      emits ATMCardActivated
    end

    command "Retire", from: ["issued", "active"] do
      role "Back office"
      goal "Take a card out of service"

      reference_to ATMCard
      given("customer is active")
      emits ATMCardRetired
    end

    # `nulls :last` (S13, ADR 0025, coverage standard) — an unnamed
    # card is real, not a gap to guess about: it sorts after every
    # named one instead of wherever a bare comparison would leave it
    # (a nil losing every "<" against a real String is the OLD,
    # accidental behavior nothing here declared on purpose).
    query "Active" do
      description "Live cards in nickname order, unnamed ones last — real nicknames sort among themselves first."
      where(status: "active")
      order_by :nickname
      nulls :last
    end

    # `offset 1` (S13, ADR 0025, coverage standard) — the second-
    # cheapest three, skipping the very cheapest: the same skip-then-
    # take `Sighting.Paged` demonstrates on the Query reference page,
    # now for real.
    query "ByFee" do
      description "Live cards by what they cost to hold, cheapest first — a fee is a Float, so the order is numeric and not alphabetical."
      where(status: "active")
      order_by :daily_fee
      limit 3
      offset 1
    end
  end

  aggregate "CardPayment" do
    given("payment is disputed") { status == "disputed" }
    given("payment is captured") { status == "captured" }
    given("payment is authorized") { status == "authorized" }
    # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED (chapter-wide sharing) — `ATMCard`'s
    # own declaration; `declared_by:` required since `Account`'s own
    # "customer is active" is a genuinely different canonical.
    given("account is open", declared_by: ATMCard)
    given("customer is active", declared_by: ATMCard)
    description "A card authorisation that either settles, is voided before settlement, or becomes a post-settlement dispute."

    reference_to Account
    # SAME NAMES ATMCard's OWN projected fields use (S12, ADR 0025) —
    # the shared given text above reads `account_status`/
    # `account_customer_status` regardless of which aggregate declares
    # it, so each `declared_by: ATMCard` consumer needs its own copy
    # under the identical field names.
    projects :account_status,          from: :"account.status"
    projects :account_customer_status, from: :"account.customer_status"
    # OPTIONAL: nil until `Dispute` actually sets it — every payment starts
    # authorized/captured with no disputant at all. `validate_relationship_
    # cardinality` (references.rb) now refuses ANY reference_to relationship
    # left nil unless told it may be, so an authorized-but-undisputed
    # CardPayment (the ordinary case) was refused at save for a fact the
    # command genuinely never set yet.
    reference_to Customer, as: :disputed_by, optional: true
    attribute :authorisation, AuthorisationCode

    identified_by :authorisation
    attribute :amount,   PaymentAmount

    value_object "AuthorisationCode" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
    end
    attribute :merchant, MerchantName

    value_object "PaymentAmount" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
      invariant("a payment amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
    end

    value_object "MerchantName" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a merchant name is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    # WHAT THE MERCHANT CATEGORY CODE SAYS ABOUT THIS CHARGE — a plain word,
    # not a closed set: the risk desk adds a tag before the language has a
    # name for it, and a scheme this narrow would refuse the very charge it
    # exists to flag.
    attribute :tags, list_of(Tag)

    value_object "Tag" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a tag is not the empty string") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "authorized" do
      transition "Capture" => "captured", from: "authorized"
      transition "Void" => "voided", from: "authorized"
      transition "Refund" => "refunded", from: "captured"
      transition "Reverse" => "reversed", from: "captured"
      transition "Dispute" => "disputed", from: ["captured", "refunded"]
      transition "Chargeback" => "charged_back", from: "disputed"
      transition "RejectDispute" => "captured", from: "disputed"
    end

    command "Authorize" do
      # DELIBERATELY LEFT ROLE-LESS — `role` is optional metadata; every
      # other command this file's own Bug #107 audit found bare now
      # declares one (payment_cards.bluebook's Capture/Void/Refund/
      # Reverse/Chargeback/RejectDispute among them), but the corpus
      # still needs at least one genuinely unguarded command for real —
      # `diagrams_spec.rb`'s own "draws nothing for a command with no
      # declared role" and `oidc_projection_spec.rb`'s own "keeps an
      # unguarded command with a nil role rather than dropping it" both
      # depend on Banking having one, by name, for a scope that must not
      # silently vanish rather than a nullable field left empty by
      # accident. Authorize stays that fixture.
      goal "Put a hold on funds for a purchase"
      attribute :authorisation, AuthorisationCode
      attribute :tags, list_of(Tag), optional: true
      # OWN GIVENS, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `account` here is
      # `Authorize`'s own fresh command argument (this creates the
      # CardPayment); see ATMCard.Issue's own comment for the full
      # reasoning, identical shape.
      given("customer is active") { account.customer.status == "active" }
      given("account is open") { account.status == "open" }
      sets :account
      sets :amount
      sets :merchant
      sets :tags
      sets :authorisation
      emits CardAuthorized
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025) — every `from:`
    # below matches a `transition` above; the removed given only
    # duplicated what `admissible_transition` already gates.
    command "Capture", from: "authorized" do
      role "System"
      goal "Turn an authorization into an actual charge"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardCaptured
    end

    command "Void", from: "authorized" do
      role "System"
      goal "Cancel an authorization before it settles"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardVoided
    end

    command "Refund", from: "captured" do
      role "System"
      goal "Give the money back after a charge settled"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardRefunded
    end

    command "Reverse", from: "captured" do
      role "System"
      goal "Undo a captured charge with no customer dispute involved"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardReversed
    end

    command "Dispute", from: ["captured", "refunded"] do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Challenge a payment that already settled"

      # The only command in the corpus carrying BOTH a self reference and a
      # cross-aggregate one, and it is here because the fact is real : a dispute
      # is raised BY someone, and on a joint account that someone is not
      # derivable from the payment. The CardPayment knows its Account and the
      # Account knows a Customer, but not which of them challenged the charge.
      #
      # Both branches of CommandBuilder#reference_to fire here. CardPayment
      # matches the owner, so it sets @references and Dispute is NOT creating ;
      # Customer does not match, so it becomes a Reference<Customer> attribute.
      # Everywhere else in the corpus those two paths are exercised apart — a
      # cross-reference always sits on a creating command or an aggregate head —
      # so nothing distinguished `creates?` reading a self-reference from
      # `creates?` reading any reference at all.
      reference_to CardPayment
      reference_to Customer, as: :disputed_by
      given("account is open")
      given("customer is active") { disputed_by.status == "active" }

      sets :disputed_by

      emits CardDisputed
    end

    command "Chargeback", from: "disputed" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Uphold a customer's dispute and claw the charge back"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardChargedBack
    end

    command "RejectDispute", from: "disputed" do
      role "Compliance officer"
      goal "Uphold the charge and close a customer's dispute"

      reference_to CardPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits CardDisputeRejected
    end

    query "Pending" do
      description "Authorized charges not yet captured, voided, or otherwise resolved."
      where(status: "authorized")
    end

    query "Disputed" do
      description "Charges currently under a customer's dispute, awaiting a compliance decision."
      where(status: "disputed")
    end

    query "Flagged" do
      description "Charges carrying a risk tag, for the fraud queue."
      where(tags: { contains: "high_risk" })
    end
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "SafeDepositBox" do
    # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED (chapter-wide sharing) — `Account`'s
    # declaration in `deposit_accounts.bluebook`, since both hold a DIRECT
    # `reference_to Customer` and so resolve the identical predicate.
    # `declared_by:` now required — `ATMCard`'s own, textually
    # different "customer is active" (reached through Account, not
    # Customer directly) also shares this chapter's own pool.
    given("customer is active", declared_by: Account)
    description "A steel box in the vault, held under one customer's name and opened only against the branch and number stamped on its face."

    belongs_to Customer

    # THE SAME LOCAL COPY Account declares (S12, ADR 0025) — a SECOND
    # real corpus member, so `projected_fields` is exercised more than
    # once (plurality_coverage_spec's own question): two independent
    # aggregates, each with their own `reference_to Customer`, each
    # copying the same remote field under the same local name by
    # coincidence of both reading "is this customer active," not by
    # any sharing this construct offers.
    projects :customer_status, from: :"customer.status"

    # A BOX NUMBER REPEATS ACROSS BRANCHES — box 12 in the downtown vault and
    # box 12 in the uptown vault are not the same box, so neither the branch
    # nor the number alone says which one this is. The first composite
    # identity in the flagship domain, carried on a head that also holds a
    # cross-reference, two entities (one of them composite in its own right),
    # and a closed set — the convergence market's Stall existed only to prove
    # was reachable at all.
    attribute :branch_code, BranchCode
    attribute :box_number,  BoxNumber

    identified_by :branch_code, :box_number
    # THE INLINE SHORTHAND, not a hand-declared value_object + one_of block —
    # AccountKind and LedgerDirection already exercise the block form
    # elsewhere in this chapter, so this is the other spelling: `one_of`
    # called directly as an attribute's type, synthesising "Size" for itself.
    attribute :size,   one_of("small", "medium", "large"), default: { value: "small" }
    attribute :visits, list_of(Visit)
    attribute :keys,   list_of(KeyIssuance)

    value_object "BranchCode" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a branch is coded") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "BoxNumber" do
      attribute :value, Integer
      invariant("a box is numbered from one") { value.positive? }
    end

    value_object "VisitSequence" do
      attribute :value, Integer
      invariant("a visit sequence is positive") { value.positive? }
    end

    value_object "VisitDate" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a visit names its date") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "VisitNote" do
      attribute :text, String
    end

    value_object "KeySerial" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a key is serialed") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    # A COMPOSITE PIECE under a composite HEAD — the same double-join market's
    # Booking exercised, and real for the same reason a booking was: a box may
    # be opened twice in one day (two visitors, or one visitor twice), so the
    # day alone does not name a visit either.
    entity "Visit" do
      description "One opening of the box, in the order it happened that day."

      attribute :date,     VisitDate
      attribute :sequence, VisitSequence

      identified_by :date, :sequence
      # MAY BE LEFT OUT — most openings are routine, and the exception is what
      # gets written down.
      attribute :note,     VisitNote, optional: true

      # A PIECE'S OWN SHAPE RULE (round 7) — `note` may be LEFT OUT
      # entirely (the comment just above), but if a vault officer
      # attaches one, an EMPTY string is not "the exception written
      # down," it is nothing written down wearing a note-shaped costume
      # — exactly the shape a VALUE OBJECT invariant on `VisitNote`
      # itself cannot express (an optional field's own VO invariant
      # never runs at all when the field is genuinely absent, which is
      # correct for absence but leaves "present, and empty" wholly
      # unchecked; only the OWNING piece, reading its own optional
      # field, can tell those two apart).
      invariant("a written note is not blank") { !note || !note.text.to_s.empty? }

      # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED (chapter-wide, ENTITY-scoped sharing)
      # — `Account::LedgerEntry`'s own declaration, in
      # deposit_accounts.bluebook, byte-identical: both read
      # `parent.customer_status == "active"` (S12, ADR 0025 — the
      # projected-field form, not a live stored-reference dereference),
      # since both pieces' own OWNING aggregate carries the identical-
      # named projected field (`projects :customer_status, from:
      # :"customer.status"`, declared once per aggregate, above/in
      # deposit_accounts.bluebook). `declared_by:` omitted — exactly
      # one piece in this chapter declares "customer is active" with a
      # block today, the same "common case" `AggregateBuilder#given`'s
      # own chapter-wide sharing already takes one level up.
      # `KeyIssuance.Return`, below, still bare-references this SAME
      # description at the COMMAND level — the existing same-aggregate
      # cross-entity pool this write-through still populates either way
      # (EntityBuilder#given_impl's own comment). Cannot reference
      # SafeDepositBox's OWN aggregate-level "customer is active"
      # instead — a genuinely different canonical (`customer_status`,
      # not `parent.customer_status`), the wrong relative path for a
      # piece's own command to evaluate.
      given("customer is active")
      given("box is rented") { parent.status == "rented" }

      lifecycle :state, default: "logged" do
        transition "Annotate" => "logged", from: "logged"
      end

      # LIFECYCLE STATE AS A COMMAND GUARD (S10, ADR 0025) — `from:`
      # replaces `given("visit is logged")`; the matching `transition`
      # above already gates the identical check via
      # `admissible_transition`.
      command "Annotate", from: "logged" do
        role "Vault officer"
        goal "Note something unusual about a visit after the fact"

        attribute :note,     VisitNote
        given("customer is active")
        given("box is rented")

        sets :note

        emits VisitAnnotated
      end

      query "Recent" do
        description "The last few visits, whatever the box has seen."
        where(state: "logged")
        limit 5
      end
    end

    # THE SECOND PIECE ON THIS HEAD, identified by a SINGLE path where Visit's
    # is two — the same deliberate mismatch market's Stall carried between
    # Booking and Inspection, so a runtime reaching for "the entity" rather
    # than the named one picks the wrong shape and says so.
    entity "KeyIssuance" do
      description "One key cut for the box, held by whoever last signed for it."

      attribute :serial, KeySerial

      identified_by :serial

      lifecycle :status, default: "issued" do
        transition "Return" => "returned", from: "issued"
      end

      command "Return" do
        role "Vault officer"
        goal "Take a key back when a holder is done with it"

        attribute :serial, KeySerial
        # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED — `Visit`'s own declaration, above,
        # shared across sibling pieces the SAME aggregate nests (the
        # cross-entity given pool a piece's own command falls back to
        # when its OWN piece declares nothing under this name).
        given("customer is active")
        given("box is rented")

        emits KeyReturned
      end
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "vacant" do
      transition "Rent"      => "rented", from: "vacant"
      transition "Surrender" => "vacant", from: "rented"
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025). `Rent`/`Surrender`
    # each match a `transition` above (redundant-but-kept, same reason
    # `Account`'s own already do both). `LogVisit`/`IssueKey` have no
    # matching transition — opening the box or cutting a key doesn't move
    # its own state — so `from:` is the ONLY thing gating them now.
    command "Rent", from: "vacant" do
      role "Branch clerk"
      goal "Assign the box to a customer"

      attribute :branch_code, BranchCode
      attribute :box_number,  BoxNumber
      attribute :size,        Size
      # OWN GIVEN, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — same reasoning as
      # Account.Open's own comment: `customer` here is `Rent`'s own
      # fresh command ARGUMENT (this creates the SafeDepositBox, so
      # `customer_status` does not exist to read yet — nothing has
      # saved this record, so nothing has seeded it). The aggregate's
      # shared "customer is active" (declared_by: Account, above)
      # reads the projected field instead, for every ACTING command
      # below this one.
      given("customer is active") { customer.status == "active" }

      sets :customer
      sets :branch_code
      sets :box_number
      sets :size

      emits BoxRented
    end

    command "Surrender", from: "rented" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Give the box back and take the keys off the account"

      reference_to SafeDepositBox

      given("customer is active")

      # TWO FACTS FROM ONE ACT, on a head that is composite-identified and
      # holds two entities — the surrender itself, and the keys it leaves
      # outstanding until the vault confirms every one of them is back.
      emits BoxSurrendered
      emits KeyReturnDue
    end

    command "LogVisit", from: "rented" do
      role "Vault officer"
      goal "Record that the box was opened"

      reference_to SafeDepositBox

      given("customer is active")

      sets :visits, append: { date: :date, sequence: :sequence, note: :note }

      emits BoxOpened
    end

    command "IssueKey", from: "rented" do
      role "Vault officer"
      goal "Cut a key for the box"

      reference_to SafeDepositBox
      given("customer is active")

      sets :keys, append: { serial: :serial }

      emits KeyIssued
    end

    query "Rented" do
      description "Boxes currently assigned to a customer, for the annual access audit."
      where(status: "rented")
      order_by :branch_code
      # A VAULT RECORD IS NOT A CASUAL READ. Named against the branch a caller
      # is standing in.
      authorize :vault_access, tenant: :branch_code
    end
  end

  # TWO POLICIES OFF ONE COMMAND'S TWO ANNOUNCEMENTS — Surrender's own comment
  # names why both facts are real; this is where each finds its audience.
  policy "ReviewOnBoxSurrender" do
    on      SafeDepositBox::BoxSurrendered
    trigger BoxSurrenderReview::Open
    across  "Compliance"
  end

  policy "FlagKeyReturn" do
    on      SafeDepositBox::KeyReturnDue
    trigger Notifications::Send
    # Undelivered on purpose — see NotifyOnClosure (deposit_accounts.bluebook).
    across  "Notifications", expect_undelivered: true
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "Statement" do
    description "A snapshot of one account's activity over one period, generated once and never revised."

    reference_to Account
    attribute :period,          StatementPeriod
    attribute :opening_balance, StatementAmount
    attribute :closing_balance, StatementAmount
    attribute :generated_on,    StatementDate
    attribute :frequency,       StatementFrequency

    # A COMPOSITE IDENTITY WHOSE FIRST PART IS A REFERENCE, not a
    # value-object field — SafeDepositBox's own composite identity
    # unwraps two single-field value objects (branch_code, box_number);
    # this is the other real shape the language allows.
    # `AttributeCollector#resolve_identity_field!` reads each field's
    # OWN declared type to decide how to reach it: `account` here is
    # `reference_to Account`'s own minted attribute (bare, no `_id` —
    # ADR 0025), already a scalar id, so it resolves bare — no value
    # object to open, the same way `Runtime::Identity.from` resolves
    # any identity head that IS a declared attribute directly.
    identified_by :account, :period

    value_object "StatementPeriod" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a statement names its period") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "StatementAmount" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
    end

    value_object "StatementDate" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a statement is dated") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    # A CLOSED SET WITH MORE THAN ONE FIELD PER MEMBER — ordinary, public
    # bare `member` lines (Vocabulary::Comparison in the self-hosted
    # grammar uses the identical shape), not a self-hosted-grammar
    # exclusive. A single-field set gets the shorter `one_of:` keyword
    # instead (LedgerDirection/AccountKind in `deposit_accounts.bluebook`) — this one can't,
    # since a member row needs to name every field, not just one.
    # `admit_member` (Runtime::Value::Admission) only
    # ever validates the DISCRIMINANT field a caller offers (`cadence`
    # here) against the members table — it does not fill the other
    # fields in for you, so a command dispatching this always states
    # every field, the same as `AddTopping`'s own append fields do.
    value_object "StatementFrequency" do
      attribute :cadence,          String
      attribute :retention_months, Integer
      attribute :paper_fee_cents,  Integer

      member cadence: "monthly",   retention_months: 84,  paper_fee_cents: 0
      member cadence: "quarterly", retention_months: 120, paper_fee_cents: 0
      member cadence: "annual",    retention_months: 240, paper_fee_cents: 500
    end

    command "Generate" do
      role "System"
      goal "Close out one period's activity into a permanent record"

      attribute :period,          StatementPeriod
      attribute :opening_balance, StatementAmount
      attribute :closing_balance, StatementAmount
      attribute :generated_on,    StatementDate
      attribute :frequency,       StatementFrequency
      # OWN GIVENS (S12, ADR 0025) — `account` is `Generate`'s own
      # fresh command argument (part of this composite-identity
      # creating command); no longer shared with ATMCard's declaration
      # since ATMCard's acting commands now read a projected field
      # nothing here would ever populate — `Generate` is Statement's
      # only command, always dispatched with a fresh `account`.
      given("customer is active") { account.customer.status == "active" }
      given("account is open") { account.status == "open" }

      sets :account
      # Wave 8 fix — these five were already declared, required command
      # attributes (identical to the aggregate's own, above) but never
      # actually written anywhere: `Generate` silently dropped every one
      # of them, leaving a Statement whose own period/balances/date/
      # frequency were always nil on the record, no matter what the
      # caller sent. Bare shorthand — each imports the already-matching
      # attribute one line up, `resolve_bare_set!`'s own comment has the
      # mechanism.
      sets :period
      sets :opening_balance
      sets :closing_balance
      sets :generated_on
      sets :frequency

      emits StatementGenerated
    end
  end

end

Hecks.bluebook "Banking" do
  aggregate "Transfer" do
    given("transfer is debited") { status == "debited" }
    # `destination_account_status`/`destination_customer_status`, not
    # `destination.status`/`destination.customer.status` (S12, ADR
    # 0025) — these are the ACTING commands' own shared givens;
    # `Request`, the creating command, keeps its own dot-path copies
    # below since `source`/`destination` there are fresh command
    # arguments, not stored state.
    given("destination account is open") { destination_account_status == "open" }
    given("destination customer is active") { destination_customer_status == "active" }
    given("transfer is requested") { status == "requested" }
    given("source account is open") { source_account_status == "open" }
    given("source customer is active") { source_customer_status == "active" }
    description "Money leaving one account for another. Two movements that must both happen, or neither."

    reference_to Account, as: :source
    reference_to Account, as: :destination

    # FOUR REAL PROJECTIONS OFF TWO ALIASED REFERENCES TO THE SAME TYPE
    # (S12, ADR 0025) — `source`/`destination` both point at Account,
    # and each carries its own local copy of that account's own
    # lifecycle field AND its own already-projected `customer_status`
    # (chaining through Account's own projection, one hop from
    # Transfer's perspective either way), entirely independent
    # declarations despite sharing a target aggregate: the DSL
    # spelling reads through the LOCAL reference name, not the
    # target's type, for exactly this reason (AggregateBuilder
    # #projects's own comment).
    projects :source_account_status,       from: :"source.status"
    projects :source_customer_status,      from: :"source.customer_status"
    projects :destination_account_status,  from: :"destination.status"
    projects :destination_customer_status, from: :"destination.customer_status"

    attribute :reference, TransferReference

    identified_by :reference

    attribute :amount,    TransferMoney

    value_object "TransferReference" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a transfer is referenced") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end
    attribute :narrative, Narrative

    value_object "TransferMoney" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
      invariant("a transfer amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
    end

    value_object "Narrative" do
      attribute :text, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'

      invariant("a transfer explains itself") { !text.to_s.empty? }
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "requested" do
      transition "Debited"  => "debited",   from: "requested"
      transition "Credited" => "credited",  from: "debited"
      transition "Settle"   => "settled",   from: "credited"
      transition "Reverse"  => "reversed",  from: "debited"
      transition "Reject"   => "rejected",  from: "requested"
    end

    command "Request" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Send money to another account"

      attribute :reference,   TransferReference

      # A REFERENCE IS THE ACCOUNT'S NUMBER, so these read it as one. They said
      # `source.value` while a reference was stored as an object wrapping that
      # number — describing the wrapper rather than the account, and a clerk
      # would not say it that way either.
      #
      # OWN GIVENS, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `source`/`destination`
      # here are `Request`'s own fresh command arguments (this creates
      # the Transfer); the acting commands' shared givens above read
      # `source_customer_status`/`source_account_status`, projected
      # fields nothing has stored until AFTER this command creates the
      # record.
      given("source customer is active") { source.customer.status == "active" }
      given("source account is open") { source.status == "open" }
      # `.empty?` rather than `.to_s.empty?` — deliberately: a valid source/
      # destination now DEREFERENCES to the referenced account's own full
      # state (CommandRules::References#dereference, needed for
      # `source.status`/`destination.status` below), and `.to_s` on that
      # Hash is not a scalar the resolver can render — `.empty?` reads
      # correctly either way, blank string or hydrated record (both
      # respond to `#empty?` with the right answer; see
      # Resolver#apply_emptiness_test).
      given("a transfer names its source")  { !source.empty? }
      given("a transfer goes somewhere")    { !destination.empty? }
      given("a transfer moves BETWEEN accounts") { source != destination }

      sets :amount
      sets :narrative
      sets :source
      sets :destination
      sets :reference

      emits TransferRequested
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025) — each `from:`
    # below matches a `transition` above; the removed given only
    # duplicated what `admissible_transition` already gates.
    command "Debited", from: "requested" do
      role "System"
      goal "Record that the source account has given up the money"

      reference_to Transfer
      given("source customer is active")
      given("source account is open")
      emits TransferDebited
    end

    command "Settle", from: "credited" do
      role "System"
      goal "Record that the destination has received it"

      reference_to Transfer
      given("destination customer is active")
      given("destination account is open")
      emits TransferSettled
    end

    command "Credited", from: "debited" do
      role "System"
      goal "Record that the destination credit committed"

      reference_to Transfer
      given("destination customer is active")
      given("destination account is open")
      emits TransferCredited
    end

    command "Reverse", from: "debited" do
      role "System"
      goal "Put the money back when the credit could not be made"

      reference_to Transfer
      given("source customer is active")
      given("source account is open")
      emits TransferReversed
    end

    command "Reject", from: "requested" do
      role "System"
      goal "Refuse a transfer before any money moved"

      reference_to Transfer
      given("source customer is active")
      given("source account is open")
      emits TransferRejected
    end

    query "InFlight" do
      description "Transfers that have left one account and not arrived at the other. The list that must always empty."
      where(status: "debited")
      order_by :status
    end
  end

  aggregate "ExternalTransfer" do
    given("transfer is sent") { status == "sent" }
    # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED — see `CardPayment`'s own comment on
    # this same reference.
    given("account is open", declared_by: ATMCard)
    given("customer is active", declared_by: ATMCard)
    # `Transfer`'s own declaration — unambiguous chapter-wide (no
    # OTHER aggregate declares a different canonical under this
    # description), so no declared_by: needed.
    given("transfer is requested")
    description "A transfer sent beyond the bank, where a recall is an instruction and a return is the external network's outcome."

    reference_to Account
    # SAME NAMES ATMCard's OWN projected fields use (S12, ADR 0025) —
    # see CardPayment's own comment on this same pattern.
    projects :account_status,          from: :"account.status"
    projects :account_customer_status, from: :"account.customer_status"
    attribute :end_to_end, EndToEndReference

    identified_by :end_to_end
    attribute :amount,      ExternalAmount
    attribute :beneficiary, BeneficiaryName
    # WHICH WAY THE MONEY MOVED ON THE ACCOUNT — and the bank already has a set
    # for that. It is the LEDGER's set, declared once on Account, so this names
    # it instead of restating it : spelling `credit`/`debit` a second time inside
    # this aggregate would be a copy of a set the domain already holds, and a
    # copy nothing compares is a copy that drifts.
    attribute :direction,   MovementDirection, admits: "Account::LedgerDirection"

    value_object "EndToEndReference" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
    end

    # A plain text holder. The VALUES it may carry are Account's business, which
    # is exactly the split `admits` exists to express: the TYPE is local, the SET
    # is named.
    value_object "MovementDirection" do
      attribute :value, String
    end

    value_object "ExternalAmount" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
      invariant("an external transfer amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
    end

    value_object "BeneficiaryName" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a beneficiary name is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "requested" do
      transition "SendTransfer" => "sent", from: "requested"
      transition "Recall" => "recalled", from: "sent"
      transition "Return" => "returned", from: "sent"
    end

    command "Request" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Send money to an account outside the bank"

      attribute :end_to_end, EndToEndReference
      # OWN GIVENS, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `account` is
      # `Request`'s own fresh command argument; see ATMCard.Issue's
      # own comment for the full reasoning.
      given("customer is active") { account.customer.status == "active" }
      given("account is open") { account.status == "open" }
      sets :account
      sets :amount
      sets :beneficiary
      sets :direction
      sets :end_to_end
      emits ExternalTransferRequested
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025) — each `from:`
