    # below matches a `transition` above.
    command "SendTransfer", from: "requested" do
      role "System"
      goal "Release the transfer to the external network"

      reference_to ExternalTransfer
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits ExternalTransferSent
    end

    command "Recall", from: "sent" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Ask the external network to stop a transfer already sent"

      reference_to ExternalTransfer
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits ExternalTransferRecalled
    end

    command "Return", from: "sent" do
      role "System"
      goal "Record that the external network sent the money back"

      reference_to ExternalTransfer
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits ExternalTransferReturned
    end

    query "Sent" do
      description "Transfers already released to the external network, awaiting its outcome."
      where(status: "sent")
    end
  end

  aggregate "ScheduledPayment" do
    given("payment is failed") { status == "failed" }
    given("payment is scheduled") { status == "scheduled" }
    # REFERENCED, NOT REDECLARED — see `CardPayment`'s own comment on
    # this same reference.
    given("account is open", declared_by: ATMCard)
    given("customer is active", declared_by: ATMCard)
    description "An instruction held for a future date, which may execute once or be cancelled before it does."

    reference_to Account
    # SAME NAMES ATMCard's OWN projected fields use (S12, ADR 0025) —
    # see CardPayment's own comment on this same pattern.
    projects :account_status,          from: :"account.status"
    projects :account_customer_status, from: :"account.customer_status"
    attribute :amount,    ScheduledAmount
    attribute :instruction, InstructionReference

    identified_by :instruction

    attribute :recipient, PaymentRecipient
    attribute :due_on,    PaymentDueDate
    attribute :attempts,     RetryCount
    attribute :max_attempts, RetryLimit

    value_object "InstructionReference" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
    end

    value_object "ScheduledAmount" do
      attribute :cents, Integer
      invariant("a scheduled payment amount is positive") { cents.positive? }
    end

    value_object "PaymentRecipient" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a payment recipient is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "PaymentDueDate" do
      attribute :value, String, pattern: '[^ \t\n\r]'
      invariant("a payment due date is present") { !value.to_s.empty? }
    end

    value_object "RetryCount" do
      attribute :value, Integer, default: 0
      invariant("a retry count is non-negative") { !value.negative? }
    end

    value_object "RetryLimit" do
      attribute :value, Integer, default: 3
      invariant("a retry limit is positive") { value.positive? }
    end

    lifecycle :status, default: "scheduled" do
      transition "Execute" => "executed",  from: "scheduled"
      transition "Cancel"  => "cancelled", from: "scheduled"
      transition "Fail"    => "failed",    from: "scheduled"
      transition "Retry"   => "failed",    from: "failed"
      transition "Abandon" => "abandoned", from: "failed"
    end

    command "Schedule" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Set up a payment to collect on a future date"

      attribute :instruction, InstructionReference
      # OWN GIVENS, NOT SHARED (S12, ADR 0025) — `account` is
      # `Schedule`'s own fresh command argument; see ATMCard.Issue's
      # own comment for the full reasoning.
      given("customer is active") { account.customer.status == "active" }
      given("account is open") { account.status == "open" }
      sets :account
      sets :amount
      sets :recipient
      sets :due_on
      sets :instruction
      emits PaymentScheduled
    end

    # LIFECYCLE STATE AS COMMAND GUARDS (S10, ADR 0025) — each `from:`
    # below matches a `transition` above.
    command "Execute", from: "scheduled" do
      role "System"
      goal "Collect a payment on its due date"

      reference_to ScheduledPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits ScheduledPaymentExecuted
    end

    command "Cancel", from: "scheduled" do
      role "Customer"
      goal "Call off a payment before its due date"

      reference_to ScheduledPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")
      emits ScheduledPaymentCancelled
    end

    command "Fail", from: "scheduled" do
      role "System"
      goal "Record that today's presentment could not be collected"

      reference_to ScheduledPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")

      emits ScheduledPaymentFailed
    end

    # SELF-TRIGGERING, ON PURPOSE — the same shape reflex.bluebook's Echo/Ring
    # proves MAX_REACTION_DEPTH with, grounded in a real rule instead of an
    # unbounded ring: an automated re-presentment against an account still
    # short of funds fails for the identical reason, so it re-announces the
    # identical event, and `RetryOnPaymentFailure` below re-enters this same
    # command. `given` is the REAL bound a bank actually enforces — a
    # schedule's own `max_attempts`, ordinarily well inside the runtime's
    # five-deep reaction ceiling, which exists as the backstop under
    # whatever a caller configures it to, not as this policy's normal exit.
    #
    # MUTATING, NOT CREATING — same reason Echo.Ring is: the reaction
    # re-dispatches this against the SAME record every time it re-enters,
    # and a creating command now refuses a second creation over one
    # identity (AlreadyExists).
    command "Retry", from: "failed" do
      role "System"
      goal "Re-present a failed payment, up to the limit the schedule names"

      reference_to ScheduledPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")

      given("a retry is still allowed") { attempts.value < max_attempts.value }

      sets :attempts, increment: { value: 1 }

      ensures("a retry never lowers the attempt count") { attempts.value == old.attempts.value + 1 }

      emits ScheduledPaymentFailed
    end

    command "Abandon", from: "failed" do
      role "Back office"
      goal "Give up on a payment that could not be collected after every retry"

      reference_to ScheduledPayment
      given("customer is active")
      given("account is open")

      given("every retry is exhausted") { attempts.value >= max_attempts.value }

      emits ScheduledPaymentAbandoned
    end

    query "Due" do
      description "Payments still scheduled, ordered by when they're due."
      where(status: "scheduled")
      order_by :due_on
    end

    policy "RetryOnPaymentFailure" do
      on      ScheduledPayment::ScheduledPaymentFailed
      trigger ScheduledPayment::Retry
    end
  end

  process_manager "Settlement" do
    # THE FIELD, NAMED — Transfer.Request declares `attribute :reference,
    # TransferReference`, which is also what Transfer's own `identified_by
    # :reference` derives its id from, so this reads the exact same scalar
    # the old bare `:transfer` reached only by coincidence (the aggregate's
    # own reference key happening to spell the same as the correlation
    # name). Named, not guessed.
    correlates_by :"reference.value"
    starts_on Transfer::TransferRequested
    ends_on   Transfer::TransferSettled

    # ONE STATE-MACHINE VOCABULARY (S7, ADR 0025) — the SAME word
    # `lifecycle`'s own `transition` already carries, one level over;
    # `state "x"` lines are gone, since every state here is already
    # named by some transition's own `from:`/target — declaring them
    # again said nothing the transitions below didn't already say.
    transition Transfer::TransferRequested => "requested", from: "requested" do
      # Debit never declared :destination — the credit leg reads it from the saga's
      # memory of the opening payload. `reference:` carries the correlation
      # forward — Account.Debit does not reference Transfer, so this is pure
      # passthrough, not an addressing key.
      #
      # `compensates` — PER-DISPATCH SAGA COMPENSATION, real bug this
      # closes: this leg's own compensation used to hang off a
      # hand-written `on :refused` list at the bottom of this saga,
      # keyed to "TransferReversed" — an event that only arrives if
      # someone dispatches `Transfer.Reverse` by hand. A destination
      # that would not take the money left the debit standing, the
      # settlement stuck in `awaiting_credit`, and the amount nowhere:
      # the reversal was written and never armed. The runtime now
      # tracks which legs actually completed and derives compensation
      # from THIS declaration directly, rather than trusting a static
      # list at the bottom to be complete and correctly ordered.
      dispatch Account::Debit, with: { number: :source, amount: :amount, narrative: { text: "transfer out" }, reference: :reference } do
        compensates Account::Credit, with: { number: :source, amount: :amount, narrative: { text: "transfer reversed" } }
      end
    end

    transition Account::AccountDebited => "awaiting_credit", from: "requested" do
      # `transfer:` HERE IS DIFFERENT — Transfer.Debited references Transfer
      # itself, so `transfer:` is its own reference key (Naming.reference_key
      # ("Banking::Transfer") == "transfer"), addressing which record to act
      # on. The VALUE stays `:reference`, reading the correlation the same
      # way every other leg does.
      #
      # NO `compensates` HERE — Account.Credit's own effect (money
      # landing in the destination) needs undoing only if something
      # LATER fails after it succeeds, which nothing in this saga does;
      # Credit is the leg most likely to refuse OUTRIGHT (a frozen
      # destination), and a leg that never completed has nothing of its
      # own to undo.
      dispatch Transfer::Debited, with: { transfer: :reference }
      dispatch Account::Credit, with: { number: :destination, amount: :amount, narrative: { text: "transfer in" }, reference: :reference }
    end

    transition Account::AccountCredited => "awaiting_credit", from: "awaiting_credit" do
      dispatch Transfer::Credited, with: { transfer: :reference }
    end

    transition Transfer::TransferCredited => "settled", from: "awaiting_credit" do
      dispatch Transfer::Settle, with: { transfer: :reference }
    end

    # `Transfer::Reverse` STAYS HAND-WRITTEN — coexistence, not
    # replacement (`ProcessManagerBuilder::HandlerBuilder#dispatch_impl`'s
    # own comment): it does not undo any ONE dispatch's own effect, it
    # marks the TRANSFER ITSELF reversed, unconditionally, whenever ANY
    # refusal lands here — a fact this saga needs regardless of which
    # leg specifically declined. Only the money movement genuinely needs
    # PER-DISPATCH compensation (`Account.Debit`'s own `compensates`,
    # above); this leg is what an empty `on :refused` body would still
    # be the right place for, if this saga ever had nothing unconditional
    # left to say here.
    transition :refused => "reversed", from: "awaiting_credit" do
      dispatch Transfer::Reverse, with: { transfer: :reference }
    end
  end

  # A SECOND SAGA, correlating on a DIFFERENT key over a DIFFERENT event
  # stream — ExternalTransfer has carried Send/Recall/Return since the chapter
  # began, and nothing ever dispatched them: a request just sat "requested"
  # until a human moved it by hand. This is the automation Settlement already
  # proved out, pointed at the network leg instead of the internal one.
  #
  # THE FIELD, NAMED — not the value object that carries it. `end_to_end` is
  # declared as a VALUE OBJECT, and a non-scalar correlation key is ambiguous
  # by construction: keying the saga on the whole object and keying it on the
  # object's rendered text are both defensible readings that correlate
  # differently. `:"end_to_end.value"` reaches past the wrapper for the one
  # scalar with a single unambiguous rendering, the same way `identified_by
  # :end_to_end` already does on the aggregate this saga watches.
  process_manager "ExternalSettlement" do
    correlates_by :"end_to_end.value"
    starts_on ExternalTransfer::ExternalTransferRequested
    ends_on   ExternalTransfer::ExternalTransferSent

    transition ExternalTransfer::ExternalTransferRequested => "requested", from: "requested" do
      dispatch ExternalTransfer::SendTransfer, with: { end_to_end: :end_to_end }
    end

    # THE COMPENSATING LEG, the same shape Settlement's own carries: a
    # refusal, not an event nothing emits, arms the return instead of leaving
    # the request stranded "requested" until someone notices.
    transition :refused => "returned", from: "requested" do
      dispatch ExternalTransfer::Return, with: { end_to_end: :end_to_end }
    end
  end

end
